subtopics.title: Cell theory: who, what, exceptions
subtopics.theory_md:
**Hooke (1665)** saw dead cork cell walls and named them "cells"; **Leeuwenhoek** first saw living cells. **Schleiden (1838)**, botanist, and **Schwann (1839)**, zoologist, proposed the **cell theory**: all organisms are made of cells, and the cell is the basic unit of structure and function. **Virchow (1855)** added *omnis cellula e cellula*: new cells arise only from pre-existing cells.

**Modern cell theory** adds: cells carry hereditary DNA passed on in division; all metabolism happens inside cells; cells are chemically alike.

**Exceptions:** viruses (acellular, need a host), coenocytes/syncytia (multinucleate, e.g. *Rhizopus*, striated muscle), mature RBCs and sieve tubes (no nucleus).
subtopics.basics_md: A cell is the smallest piece that can live on its own. The theory says every living thing is built from these pieces and that a new piece can only be made by an old piece splitting.

subtopics.title: Why cells are small; attributes of life
subtopics.theory_md:
A cell takes in nutrients and removes waste through its **surface**, but its demand grows with its **volume**. For a sphere
$$\frac{SA}{V}=\frac{4\pi r^2}{\tfrac43\pi r^3}=\frac{3}{r}$$
so the ratio falls as the cell grows. Past a limit the surface cannot feed the volume, so the cell **divides** (or folds its surface: microvilli, ER).

**Attributes of life:** cellular organisation, metabolism, growth, reproduction, response to stimuli, homeostasis, heredity and evolution. About 1.7 to 2 million species are described; insects (about 1 million) are the largest group.
subtopics.basics_md: Food comes in through the skin of the cell but has to feed the whole inside. A bigger ball has relatively less skin per bit of inside, so there is a size where it cannot cope.
key_points: SA/V = 3/r for a sphere; falls as r grows
Uptake is by surface, need is by volume
Large cell divides to restore SA/V
Life: cells, metabolism, growth, reproduction, response, homeostasis, heredity

subtopics.title: Plasma membrane, nucleus and ribosomes
subtopics.theory_md:
**Plasma membrane:** fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins; it **regulates movement** of substances, allows cell communication and recognition. It does not make ATP in eukaryotes and does not give mechanical support (the wall does that in plants).

**Nucleus:** double envelope with pores, chromatin (DNA), **nucleolus**. The nucleolus makes **rRNA** and assembles ribosomal subunits.

**Ribosomes:** rRNA and protein, no membrane; the site of **protein synthesis (translation)** in both prokaryotes (70S) and eukaryotes (80S).
subtopics.basics_md: The membrane is the cell's gate, the nucleus is its office holding the plans, and ribosomes are the machines that follow the plans to build proteins.

subtopics.title: ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles
subtopics.theory_md:
**RER** (ribosomes) makes proteins for secretion and membranes; **SER** makes lipids and steroids and detoxifies.

**Golgi:** a stack of cisternae; **cis face** receives from the ER, **trans face** ships out. It modifies (glycosylation), sorts and packages proteins, and forms lysosomes. It is the organelle that packages and modifies proteins before secretion.

**Lysosomes:** single-membrane vesicles of acid hydrolases (pH about 5): digest food, bacteria and worn-out organelles (**autophagy**); "suicide bags".

**Vacuoles:** store water, salts and wastes; the large plant vacuole keeps turgor.

subtopics.title: Mitochondria and the electron transport system
subtopics.theory_md:
**Mitochondria:** double membrane, inner membrane folded into **cristae**, matrix with circular DNA and 70S ribosomes. The **powerhouse**: Krebs cycle in the matrix, ETS and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane make most of the ATP.

**ETS:** Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) and II (succinate dehydrogenase) $\rightarrow$ ubiquinone $\rightarrow$ III ($bc_1$) $\rightarrow$ cytochrome c $\rightarrow$ IV (cytochrome oxidase) $\rightarrow$ $\mathrm{O_2}$ gives $\mathrm{H_2O}$. $\mathrm{H^+}$ pumped across the inner membrane drives ATP synthase (chemiosmosis).

**Malate-aspartate shuttle:** cytosolic NADH cannot cross the inner membrane, so malate carries its reducing power in and aspartate returns.
subtopics.basics_md: Food is burned slowly in steps. The energy released moves protons across a membrane, and when they flow back through ATP synthase they make ATP, like water turning a turbine.

subtopics.title: The cell cycle and its control
subtopics.theory_md:
The **cell cycle** is the ordered sequence of events by which a cell grows, duplicates its DNA and divides. About 24 h in a human cell.

**Interphase:** $G_1$ (cell growth, protein and RNA synthesis, preparation for DNA synthesis), **S** (DNA replication, $2C\to4C$, chromosome number still $2n$), $G_2$ (grows, makes spindle proteins). **M phase:** mitosis then cytokinesis. $G_0$: resting.

**Control:** cyclins and CDKs at checkpoints ($G_1/S$, $G_2/M$, metaphase). **p53** and **Rb** stop damaged cells; loss of these or oncogene activation gives uncontrolled division, i.e. **cancer**.
subtopics.basics_md: A cell goes through a loop: grow, copy its DNA, check the copy, split. Checkpoints are inspectors that stop the loop if something is wrong.
key_points: Cell cycle = interphase (G1, S, G2) + M phase
G1: growth; S: DNA replication; G2: preparation for mitosis

subtopics.title: Mitosis, cytokinesis and the spindle
subtopics.theory_md:
Mitosis is **equational** division: $2n\to2n$, two identical daughters (growth, repair).

- **Prophase:** chromatin condenses, nucleolus and envelope disappear, spindle forms.
- **Metaphase:** chromosomes align at the equator, spindle fibres attached to kinetochores.
- **Anaphase:** centromeres split, sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles.
- **Telophase:** chromosomes decondense, envelope and nucleolus reappear.

**Karyokinesis** is division of the nucleus; **cytokinesis** divides the cytoplasm. Animals: **cleavage furrow** (actin-myosin ring, outside in). Plants: **cell plate** from Golgi vesicles (inside out), becoming the new wall.

**Spindle fibres** are microtubules; if they fail, chromosomes missegregate (aneuploidy).
subtopics.basics_md: The cell copies its chromosomes, lines them up, pulls one copy of each to each end, and then pinches the cell in two.

subtopics.title: Meiosis and how it differs from mitosis
subtopics.theory_md:
Meiosis is **reductional** division in germ cells: one $2n$ cell makes **four haploid ($n$) cells** by two divisions with one DNA replication.

**Meiosis I:** Prophase I (leptotene, **zygotene** synapsis and bivalents, **pachytene** crossing over, **diplotene** chiasmata, diakinesis), Metaphase I (bivalents at equator), **Anaphase I (homologues separate; centromeres do not split)**, Telophase I. **Meiosis II** is like mitosis (sister chromatids separate).

**Significance:** keeps the chromosome number constant over generations, and gives **variation** through crossing over and random assortment.

| | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Cells | somatic | germ |
| Divisions | one | two |
| Products | 2, $2n$, identical | 4, $n$, different |
subtopics.basics_md: Eggs and sperm must carry half the chromosomes, otherwise the number would double every generation. Meiosis does the halving and shuffles genes while it is at it.

subtopics.title: Binary fission and the bacterial growth curve
subtopics.theory_md:
**Binary fission:** bacteria copy the single circular chromosome, attach the copies to the membrane, elongate, and form a septum: two identical cells in about 20 min. There is **no nucleus, no spindle and no distinct stages** (mitosis has all three).

**Growth curve** (log of cell number against time): **lag** (cells adapt to the medium, make enzymes and ribosomes, **no increase in number**), **exponential or log** (doubling every generation time $g$, $N=N_02^{n}$, the straight-line part of the log plot), **stationary** (growth equals death, nutrients run out), **death**.
subtopics.basics_md: Bacteria simply copy their one loop of DNA and split. When put in fresh food, they first get ready (lag), then double again and again (log), then run out of food.

subtopics.title: Carbohydrates, glycosidic bond, body elements
subtopics.theory_md:
**Elements:** O (65%), C (18%), H (10%), N (3%) make about 96% of body mass.

**Carbohydrates** are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, $\mathrm{C_n(H_2O)_n}$. By monomer units: **monosaccharides** (glucose, fructose, galactose, ribose); **disaccharides** (sucrose = glucose + fructose, lactose = glucose + galactose, maltose = glucose + glucose); **polysaccharides** (starch in plants, **glycogen** in animals, cellulose, chitin).

A **glycosidic bond** is the C-O-C link formed by dehydration between two sugars; found in di- and polysaccharides.

Functions: energy (4 kcal/g), storage, structure, cell recognition. Carbohydrates (with fats) give energy; proteins build the body. Catalysis is by enzymes, not carbohydrates.

subtopics.title: Proteins: structure, denaturation, disorders
subtopics.theory_md:
Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by **peptide bonds**.
- **Primary:** amino acid sequence (decided by the gene). A mutation changes it and so can change function.
- **Secondary:** $\alpha$-helix and $\beta$-sheet held by **hydrogen bonds** between backbone C=O and N-H.
- **Tertiary:** 3-D fold of one chain (disulphide bonds, ionic, hydrophobic).
- **Quaternary:** several chains (haemoglobin).

**Denaturation:** loss of secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure by heat, extreme pH, urea, solvents, heavy metals; peptide bonds and primary structure stay.

**Disorders:** sickle-cell anaemia (Glu to Val), Alzheimer's (amyloid-$\beta$), Parkinson's ($\alpha$-synuclein), prion diseases, cystic fibrosis (CFTR misfold). Scurvy: vitamin C deficiency affects collagen.
subtopics.basics_md: A protein is a string of beads (amino acids) that folds into a precise shape. The shape does the job, so a wrong bead or a lost fold stops it working.
key_points: Primary = sequence by peptide bonds; secondary = H-bonds (helix, sheet)
Tertiary = 3-D fold; quaternary = several chains

subtopics.title: DNA, RNA, gene and genome
subtopics.theory_md:
**Nucleotide** = sugar + base + phosphate. Nucleotides join by **phosphodiester bonds** (phosphate linking 3' of one sugar to 5' of the next).

**DNA (Watson-Crick):** two **antiparallel** strands in a right-handed double helix; backbone outside, bases inside; A=T (2 H-bonds), G$\equiv$C (3); 10 bp and 3.4 nm per turn. **Stable store of genetic information** and template for replication.

|---|---|---|
| Sugar | deoxyribose | ribose |
| Base | thymine | **uracil** |
| Strands | double | single |

**RNA types:** **mRNA** carries the code; **tRNA** brings amino acids to the ribosome; **rRNA** forms ribosomes. **Gene** = DNA segment coding for one product; **genome** = complete DNA of an organism.

subtopics.title: Glycolysis
subtopics.theory_md:
**Glycolysis** (EMP pathway): cytoplasm, no $\mathrm{O_2}$ needed. **One glucose (6C) gives two pyruvate (3C).**

**Investment:** glucose $\rightarrow$ G6P (**hexokinase**, $-1$ ATP) $\rightarrow$ F6P (isomerase) $\rightarrow$ F1,6BP (**PFK-1**, $-1$ ATP) $\rightarrow$ G3P + DHAP (aldolase).
**Pay-off (x2):** G3P $\rightarrow$ 1,3BPG (G3P dehydrogenase, **NADH**) $\rightarrow$ 3PG (phosphoglycerate kinase, **ATP**) $\rightarrow$ 2PG (mutase) $\rightarrow$ PEP (enolase) $\rightarrow$ pyruvate (**pyruvate kinase**, ATP).

Net: 2 ATP + 2 NADH ($=8$ ATP with NADH $=3$). Without $\mathrm{O_2}$: pyruvate $\rightarrow$ lactate or ethanol.
subtopics.basics_md: Glucose is split into two halves in the cytoplasm. Two ATP are spent to start, four are made, so the net gain is two, plus two NADH for later.

subtopics.title: Krebs cycle and energy balance
subtopics.theory_md:
**Link reaction** (matrix, pyruvate dehydrogenase): pyruvate $\rightarrow$ acetyl-CoA + $\mathrm{CO_2}$ + NADH.

**Krebs cycle** (matrix), per acetyl-CoA: acetyl-CoA (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) $\rightarrow$ **citrate** (6C) $\rightarrow$ isocitrate $\rightarrow$ $\alpha$-ketoglutarate (5C; $\mathrm{CO_2}$, NADH) $\rightarrow$ succinyl-CoA (4C; $\mathrm{CO_2}$, NADH) $\rightarrow$ succinate (GTP) $\rightarrow$ fumarate ($\mathrm{FADH_2}$) $\rightarrow$ malate $\rightarrow$ oxaloacetate (NADH).

Per turn: **3 NADH, 1 $\mathrm{FADH_2}$, 1 GTP, 2 $\mathrm{CO_2}$**. Per glucose, 2 turns.

NCERT (NADH 3, $\mathrm{FADH_2}$ 2): glycolysis 8 + link 6 + Krebs 24 = **38 ATP**. Modern (2.5, 1.5): about 30 to 32.
